title:
Letter from St.
                      Petersburg
author: Modern
content:
These notes from a trip to St. Petersburg two years ago were included in a letter to a friend.

PROVIDENCE, JUNE 27, 1994

D
EAR J,

  Pressed for time before leaving for Russia, I tried loyally to send you a postcard while we waited for our bus to the airport.  I fed my dollar bill into the stamp vending machine and got... nothing.  A good enough prelude to Russia, I suppose.

  In St. Petersburg I also tried to buy stamps at the main post office.  I got in the line at the international mail counter, and waited.  There was no one behind the counter, but there were so many people waiting that I figured someone would show up eventually.  No one ever did, although there was a cat sleeping on the information counter.  I left, figuring that mail sent in America after I returned would get to you faster anyway.  Here are some thoughts written down during the trip, in roughly postcard-size bites:

  Looking around the skyline of St. Petersburg, it seems that every time the Soviets needed a new construction crane they simply built a new one on the spot, and abandoned it when the project was finished.  Dozens, maybe hundreds, of these huge stationary cranes and lots of other kinds of heavy machinery are scattered around the city and they never seem to move.

  Two years ago the price of a metro token in Moscow was one rouble, a little less than an American penny.  Here the price has risen to 150 roubles, about 13 American cents.  A loaf of bread costs 300 roubles.  There has been no corresponding rise in most people's salaries.  An old woman working at the palace museum in Pavlovsk-- a woman who had spent time in a German camp during the Siege-- said she earns 30,000 roubles a month.

  Cars drive so fast on Nevsky Prospekt, the main street downtown, that little old women have to sprint from one side to the other.

  Russians love books.  In spite of Russia's inflation rate, the salesladies at a used-book store on Nevsky Prospekt write prices in ink inside the back covers of most of their inventory.  Evidently, even at prices of at least one thousand roubles, the books sell so quickly that inflation isn't a problem.

  We saw one of the ubiquitous construction cranes actually moving this afternoon.  We were afraid to walk beneath it.

  On the door of the nearest supermarket hangs a photo of a dishevelled Vladimir Zhirinovsky with the slogan "I will lift Russia off her knees."  I look around in the subway sometimes and try to guess who votes for him.

  We planned to go to the Hermitage today but we turned away when we discovered that the price for foreign tourists was 16,000 roubles-- about 50 times more than the 300-rouble price for Russians, plus another 9000 roubles for the right to take pictures.  In this country, of course, 16,000 roubles isn't much for a Western tourist.  It's about eight dollars, which is what you might pay to get into a good museum in the West.  The problem is, it's insulting.  This isn't the West, the Hermitage isn't a Western-quality museum, and the money will probably go straight into the hands of the mafia anyway.  It's as if an American museum charged Americans two dollars to get in, and foreigners, $100.  The only reason they charge these prices is because they can usually get away with it.

  "This should be interesting," David said as we waited for the train in a thick crowd of people in the Gostiny Dvor metro station.  The train arrived, the doors opened, and an equally dense mass of people started to squeeze out.  When they finished, only five or ten seconds remained until the doors closed again, so we all started to push in.  David made it before I did, and, fearing that I would be left behind or caught in the closing doors, I reached over the heads of the people in front of me, grabbed a metal hand-hold, and pulled myself in.  Still more people managed to squeeze in, until we were crushed in so tightly that I was nearly lifted off the floor.  All this was impressive enough, but the most memorable sight was that in the midst of all these people, crammed in so tightly that we couldn't even turn around, a man stood completely absorbed in a hand-held video game: Brick Boy.  I'm not sure if he even noticed the crowd.

  Unlike two years ago (at least in Central Asia) when the gangsters were still pretty new at their trade and identified themselves only by wearing black T-shirts with the names of Western brands like GUCCI stitched on in primary colors, this year the Russian mafiosi are wearing sportsjackets with plain T-shirts or turtlenecks.  You can see them all over Nevsky Prospekt, usually in pairs, or driving their Mercedes Benzes, their car of choice.  Some of them look pretty amateurish.  At the age of maybe 17 or 18, they walk around in slightly mismatched costumes, with pants that are too short and shoes that seemed designed by Soviet planners to look goofy.  Some of them are geniunely getting rich though, and are probably dangerous.  Lyubov Alekseevna, one of our former Russian teachers, told us last night that more Rolls Royces, another favorite mafia car, are sold in Russia now than in the rest of Europe put together.  David and I were sitting in front of the Kazansky Sobor (a prominent cathedral, now unbelievably dingy) on Thursday and he decided to take a picture of two mafia boys who were walking by.  These two looked relatively innocent, and David tried to look like he was taking a snapshot of the whole street in general, but one of them noticed us, and kept turning back to look at us through his dark glasses.

  Yesterday was the day of malfunctions.  We re-enacted our crowded-metro scene this afternoon, only this time the train stopped two feet out of alignment with the metro station doors that are supposed to open at the same time as the train doors, and there was no light at all in our metro car.  Riding the metro in the dark felt like an amusement park attraction, but we also couldn't help but think of darkened, crowded railroad cars leading people off to forced-labor camps or worse.  If the Russians were reminded of this, though, they didn't show it and the young people just giggled.  The next calamity happened in Lyubov's kitchen.  While we were talking after dinner, the light bulb in a hanging lamp decided to explode spectacularly, dropping shards of broken glass all over the floor.  "Nobody get up!  Nobody get up!" she said as she went for a broom.  Finally, near midnight, Lyubov packed us onto trolleybus number 50, promising that it would eventually take us to a metro stop one away from where we were staying.  We would have preferred to take the more predictable metro the whole way, even if it took longer, but all we could do was trust her.

  Naturally, something went wrong.  After about ten or fifteen minutes the trolleybus stopped and the driver simply said, in the same tone he used to announce the name of each stop, "trollejbus slomalsa"-- the trolleybus broke.  With no comment, anger or disapointment, everyone calmly got up and left, as if this happens all the time.  Luckily we broke down right near another metro stop, and so in another hour or so we were able to get home.  I had already laughed earlier in the day at a sign warning people to stay away from a closed escalator, saying that it was "Opasno dlia zhizni"-- which translates literally as "life-threatening," a sign that should probably be everywhere here.  As we arrived at our home metro stop, David mimicked the recorded voice from the metro cars that warns you about the closing doors: "Ostorozhno!  Vy v Rossii." -- "Caution!  You are in Russia."

  On Thursday we ate at Pickwick's, an Indian restaurant.  Located a couple of blocks behind the Kazansky Sobor, it's the best restaurant we know of in the in the whole city, so David asked the manager which days of the week they were closed so we could plan to come back.  The manager told us unequivocally that they had no days off, and he even reassured us when we specifically asked if they would be open on Saturday and Sunday.  So we went to eat there this afternoon, Sunday, and of course they were closed, with a chain and padlock across the doors.  We went upstars to a bar which displayed a few menu items such as a sandvich, a khot dog and a gamburger, but these samples lay under a plastic cover and they reminded me a little too much of Peter the Great's formaldehyde collection of malformed, stillborn infants which we had just seen at the ethnological and anthropological museum.  "Last Sunday we had khachipuri (cheese pies) at that stand by Spasna Krovi.  They're probably open," I said, wondering immediately if I should have gotten our hopes up with this kind of prediction.  They too were closed, but luckily we found a Western supermarket on Nevsky.  We bought milk, sausage, a Snickers bar and Tyson's frozen breaded chicken breasts.

  The view from the kitchen window of the apartment were we are staying shows us a gray supermarket with nothing at all displayed in its windows; a collection of closed, makeshift kiosks which, when they are open, usually carry a greater variety of goods than the supermarket; two rusty green quonset huts for unknown purposes; a trench at least 200 yards long which lays bare a section of pipe (an orange crane is parked beside it but no work at all has been done the whole time we have been here); a statue of Prometheus, a Communist favorite; about four dozen dingy concrete apartment buildings which even in this relatively nice section of town (because it is not completely strewn with trash) might qualify as housing projects in America; three idle construction cranes; a small amusement park which plays the same tape of Western pop songs over and over all day via a loudspeaker; six widely-spaced upright slabs of concrete serving no obvious purpose in a parking lot; a turned-over, rusty, yellow, unidentifiable piece of metro equipment; an overgrown clearing of trees where garbage is periodically burned; the back of the LenExpo building, where an exhibition of goods from Slovakia is being held this week; a large movie theater with two of its three ticket windows abandoned, and with large windows hung with thin, crooked, mismatched curtains but occasionally displaying the wares of a second-hand clothing store which now resides within the theater lobby.

  It is near 11 p.m. and the sun hasn't set yet.  Someone just stopped and picked lilacs off the bushes in front of the theater.
